steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper asking whether visual grounding helps neural language models learn word meanings, especially with little data. Motivate it from LMs as cognitive models and the data gap with children, describe the models and evaluations we use, and summarize the findings.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. LMs as models of human language processing, and the data-efficiency gap
2. Grounding in perception; multi-modal models
3. This paper: models, controlled training, evaluation suite
4. Findings
5. Conclusion: what this means for grounded language acquisition

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. LMs and human language
- LMs: remarkable success across many language tasks (cite)
- useful for predicting human language processing: behavioral models of production (cite), comprehension (cite), neural responses to linguistic input (cite)
- strong candidates as computational models of human language processing
- but implausible as models of cognitive development: training data far exceeds what learners receive (cite)
- tens of billions of sentences vs around a million sentences in first three years (cite)
- human-like LM learning -> richer models of language acquisition, child learning dynamics; maybe more sample-efficient NLP

2. Grounding
- humans ground language in perception across modalities: vision, touch, hearing (cite)
- sighted learners: vision hypothesized central, detailed info often directly coupled to linguistic input (cite)
- NLP researchers: multi-modal training as path to human-like learning (cite)
- many recent multi-modal models/algorithms, mostly for tasks reasoning over both modalities (cite)
- whether they gain human-like learning efficiency of language: little attention

3. This paper
- does visual grounding improve word learning in neural LMs?
- models: CLIP (cite), GIT (cite), Flamingo (cite); very different ways of fusing vision and language
- control and vary dataset size and within-language distributional info (word co-occurrence statistics)
- evaluation suite: syntactic categories, lexical relations, semantic features, semantic similarity, human neural representations

4. Findings
- grounded learning better than language-only controls on word similarity and semantic features
- only with datasets small even by human-learning standards
- only when limiting word co-occurrence exposure; sometimes reduced sample efficiency with images + captions vs images + single words
- visual and distributional info partially complementary, but no model integrates both to improve word representations

5. Conclusion
- current models/training far from models of visually grounded language acquisition
- grounding helps some but not all aspects of semantics; distributional info can override (maybe interfere with) grounded learning

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Neural language models (LMs) have been remarkably successful on a wide variety of language processing tasks. They have also been useful for predicting aspects of human language processing, in behavioral models of production and comprehension and also in models of neural responses to linguistic inputs. So LMs are strong candidates for computational models of core aspects of human language processing. However, right now these models are very implausible as models of human cognitive development. Effective LMs need much more training data than the linguistic input human language learners get during development: modern LMs are usually trained on tens of billions of sentences, but children only get around a million sentences in the first three years of their lives. If we had techniques for building LMs that learn like humans, this would immediately make richer computational models of language acquisition and child language learning dynamics possible, and maybe also give a path to more sample-efficient learning in LMs for NLP applications.

A very significant difference between how humans and LMs learn language is that humans ground language in perceptual signals from many different modalities, like vision, touch, and hearing. For sighted learners, vision is hypothesized to play a central role, because it gives detailed information that is often directly coupled to the linguistic input. Researchers in natural language processing have argued that multi-modal training might be a path toward more human-like language learning. In recent years many multi-modal models and learning algorithms have been introduced, which is promising, and they are mostly targeted at tasks that need reasoning about data in both modalities at the same time. But not much attention has been paid to how far these models actually get more human-like learning efficiency for language itself.

3. This paper
- does visual grounding improve word learning in neural LMs?
- models: CLIP, GIT, Flamingo; very different ways of fusing vision and language
- control and vary dataset size and within-language distributional info (word co-occurrence statistics)
- evaluation suite: syntactic categories, lexical relations, semantic features, semantic similarity, human neural representations

- only with datasets small even by human-learning standards
- only when limiting word co-occurrence exposure; sometimes reduced sample efficiency with images + captions vs images + single words

- current models/training far from models of visually grounded language acquisition

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Neural language models (LMs) have been remarkably successful on a wide variety of language processing tasks. They have also been useful for predicting aspects of human language processing, in behavioral models of production and comprehension and also in models of neural responses to linguistic inputs. So LMs are strong candidates for computational models of core aspects of human language processing. However, right now these models are very implausible as models of human cognitive development. Effective LMs need much more training data than the linguistic input human language learners get during development: modern LMs are usually trained on tens of billions of sentences, but children only get around a million sentences in the first three years of their lives. If we had techniques for building LMs that learn like humans, this would immediately make richer computational models of language acquisition and child language learning dynamics possible, and maybe also give a path to more sample-efficient learning in LMs for NLP applications.

A very significant difference between how humans and LMs learn language is that humans ground language in perceptual signals from many different modalities, like vision, touch, and hearing. For sighted learners, vision is hypothesized to play a central role, because it gives detailed information that is often directly coupled to the linguistic input. Researchers in natural language processing have argued that multi-modal training might be a path toward more human-like language learning. In recent years many multi-modal models and learning algorithms have been introduced, which is promising, and they are mostly targeted at tasks that need reasoning about data in both modalities at the same time. But not much attention has been paid to how far these models actually get more human-like learning efficiency for language itself.

In this paper we look at whether visual grounding can improve a key aspect of language understanding in neural LMs, namely word learning. We study several visually grounded models, including CLIP, GIT, and Flamingo, which fuse vision and language data in drastically different ways. When training these models we carefully control and systematically vary both the dataset size and the amount of within-language distributional information given by word co-occurrence statistics. Then we characterize the models with a suite of tasks that benchmark different facets of word knowledge, by predicting syntactic categories, lexical relations, semantic features, semantic similarity, and human neural representations.

We find that grounded word learning can indeed give better performance than the language-only control models in capturing word similarity and semantic features. But we only see this benefit when training on datasets that are small even by the standards of human learning. More surprisingly, we only see it when the models' exposure to word co-occurrence information within language is limited: in some cases models even show reduced sample efficiency when learning from images and captions compared to images with single words. Further analyses show that visual and distributional information are partially complementary, but none of the models we study can integrate both perceptual and textual contexts to get better word representations.

Our results suggest that current models and training procedures are still far from being models of visually grounded language acquisition. Grounding can help these models learn some aspects of semantics, but not all, and the distributional information in language can override (and maybe interfere with) visually grounded learning.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Neural language models (LMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide variety of language processing tasks [1,2,3,4]. They have also proven useful for predicting aspects of human language processing, both in behavioral models of production [5] and comprehension [6] and in models of neural responses to linguistic inputs [7,8,9]. LMs are therefore strong candidates as computational models of core aspects of human language processing. At present, however, these models are profoundly implausible as models of human cognitive development. The amount of training data required by effective LMs greatly exceeds the linguistic input that human language learners receive during development [10,11]: modern LMs are typically trained on tens of billions of sentences, whereas children receive only around a million sentences in the first three years of their lives [12]. Techniques for building LMs that learn like humans would immediately enable richer computational models of language acquisition and child language learning dynamics, and might offer a path toward more sample-efficient learning in LMs targeted at NLP applications.

One of the most significant differences between how humans and LMs learn language is that humans ground language in perceptual signals spanning many modalities, including vision, touch, and hearing [13,14,15,16]. In sighted learners, vision is hypothesized to play a central role, since it delivers detailed information that is often directly coupled to linguistic input [17]. Researchers in the natural language processing community have argued that multi-modal training might offer a path toward more human-like language learning [18]. Promisingly, recent years have seen a profusion of multi-modal models and learning algorithms, mostly targeted at tasks that require reasoning about data in both modalities simultaneously [19,20,21,22,23]. However, the extent to which these models actually acquire more human-like learning efficiency of language itself has received limited attention.

In this paper, we investigate whether visual grounding can improve a key aspect of language understanding, word learning, in neural LMs. We study a variety of visually grounded models, including CLIP [19], GIT [20], and Flamingo [21], which represent drastically different ways of fusing vision and language data. While training these models, we carefully control and systematically vary both dataset size and the amount of within-language distributional information provided by word co-occurrence statistics. We then characterize the models with a suite of tasks designed to benchmark various facets of word knowledge, via prediction of syntactic categories, lexical relations, semantic features, semantic similarity, and human neural representations.

We find that grounded word learning can indeed yield better performance than the control language-only models in capturing word similarity and semantic features. However, this benefit is observed only when training on datasets that are small even by the standards of human learning. More surprisingly, it is observed only when models' exposure to word co-occurrence information within language is limited: in some cases, models actually exhibit reduced sample efficiency when learning from images and captions rather than images accompanied by single words. Although further analyses show that visual and distributional information are partially complementary, none of the models we study can integrate both perceptual and textual contexts to yield improved word representations.

Our results suggest that current models and training procedures remain far from serving as models of visually grounded language acquisition. In these models, grounding can facilitate learning of some, but not all, aspects of semantics, while distributional information contained within language can override (and perhaps interfere with) visually grounded learning.
